newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel demands Egypt stop threatening it.
newsitem.headline: Israel demands Egypt stop threatening it.

text.p: Israel's right-wing government demanded on Tuesday that Egypt stop "threatening" it for taking a slower approach to peace than its Labour-led predecessor.

Asked if Egypt could play a key peacemaking role in the present atmosphere, Foreign Minister David Levy told reporters: "If Egypt continues to express itself this way, it is effectively not interested."
Afterwards Levy said Israel expected Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak to change the atmosphere. He demanded Egypt "break up this threatening cloud."

Levy summoned Egyptian Ambassador Mohammed Bassiouny to his office to complain about heightened rhetoric levelled against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Likud-led government which took office three months ago.

Netanyahu, who on Tuesday embarked on his first European diplomatic tour since his May election, told reporters on his plane he hoped Eygpt would act in the spirit of its 1979 peace treaty with Israel.
"I expect Egypt to act in the spirit of the peace agreements...actions and friendship that characterise a country that signed a peace agreement with us," he said.
"There is no place for verbal escalation that has come from Egypt lately. I hope they will find a different way to express their opinion."

On Tuesday, the London-based Arabic newspaper Asharq al-Awsat quoted Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, in the latest salvo, as saying Israel's expectations from peace talks were "nonsense," plausible only to the ignorant or mad.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh rushed to Netanyahu's defence, insisting the government was conducting negotiations with Palestinians "more carefully", "more responsibly" and "not as quickly" as the left-centre government it ousted.

As progress, Naveh cited a series of meetings between Israeli and Palestinian leaders. But Bassiouny said he hoped a joint Israeli-Palestinian steering committee meeting on Thursday would lead to "tangible steps on the ground."
Egypt has complained about Israel's failure to hand over parts of the West Bank city of Hebron to self-rule as agreed in peace deals with the Palestinians or to expand talks with them.
Mubarak had welcomed Netanyahu when they first met in Cairo shortly after the Israeli leader took office. The Egyptian president said at the time he had "great hopes."
But Egypt's mood soured with a lack of progress in peace talks, and it threatened to cancel a Middle East economic conference scheduled for Cairo in November.

Last week Netanyahu said that to cancel the conference would hurt Cairo. Educated in the United States, he used an English expression, likening any Egyptian cancellation to "a man who cuts off his nose to spite his face."
At the time Moussa reacted angrily, calling Netanyahu's comment "unfortunate" and warning Netanyahu: "He'd do best to keep off Egypt's nose so that Egypt keeps off his nose."
On Monday, Moussa's assistant foreign minister, Fathi el-Shazli said Israeli leaders were talking like "dinosaurs" and were amateur politicians.
Bassiouny denied it was Egyptian policy to attack personalities. He said Egypt would express its views freely. He said an atmosphere of peace was necessary for the economic conference to succeed.
"How can you convince the foreign investors to invest in this area in which there is no stability?" he asked.
